cards.say: You don't need to write code to lead AI work well. You need to know what it's actually good at, what it costs, and where the risk sits.

cards.q: Which question matters most before approving an AI project?
options: What's the flashiest demo we can show?
What decision or task does this improve, and how will we know?
Which vendor has the biggest marketing budget?
cards.why: A clear, measurable improvement beats an impressive demo. If you can't state what gets better, the project isn't ready to fund.

cards.q: One line here is a red flag in a project pitch. Tap it.
sentences: The team can name the metric this is expected to move.
The team says accuracy will "just get better over time", with no plan for how.
The team has a plan for what happens when the model is wrong.
cards.why: "It'll improve" isn't a plan. Ask how, by when, and what happens if it doesn't.

cards.q: Match the role to what it mainly brings to an AI project
pairs: Knows what a right answer actually looks like
Decides what oversight the use case needs
Owns the budget and the outcome
cards.why: AI projects usually stall from a missing role, not from a weak model.

cards.q: A team wants to ship an AI feature with no way to check its accuracy after launch. What's your call?
options: Ask for a way to catch errors before it ships
cards.why: You don't need to block AI work to lead it responsibly, you need a way to catch problems. That's usually a small ask that saves a much larger cleanup later.
